analysis.one_liner: Requires railroads to install defect detectors, inspect hazmat cars, and pay much larger safety fines.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Ohio bill to tighten freight rail safety after the East Palestine derailment was referred to committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The RAIL Act would have required the Transportation Department to write new safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials: advance notice to state emergency planners, fewer blocked road crossings, limits on train length and weight, and a hotbox detector — the device that spots overheating wheel bearings, the failure that caused the East Palestine derailment — every 10 miles. It would also raise maximum safety fines tenfold, mandate more thorough rail car inspections, move up the retirement of older tank cars by a year, and charge each big railroad $1 million a year to fund first-responder training grants. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along freight rail lines where trains carry hazardous materials, local firefighters and emergency responders who need training and information about what is coming through their towns, and rail workers who perform inspections.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a federally regulated wayside defect detector — including a hotbox detector to catch overheating wheel bearings — every 10 miles of track over which hazmat trains run, and spells out what crews must do when a detector sounds an alert [S2] [S3].

Requires railroads to give state and tribal emergency-response officials advance notice of hazardous materials moving through their areas, including a written gas discharge plan, and to reduce blocked road crossings [S2] [S3].

Raises the maximum federal fine for rail safety violations from $75,000 and $175,000 to the greater of $750,000 and $1,750,000 or a percentage of the carrier's annual income, so penalties are large enough to matter to big railroads [S3].
Charges each Class I (largest) railroad a $1 million annual fee and doubles the cap on supplemental training grants to fund hazmat training for local first responders [S3].

Requires qualified mechanical inspectors to spend a minimum time on each rail car carrying hazardous materials, ends the abbreviated pre-departure inspection for those cars, and moves the phase-out of older DOT-111 tank cars up one year to May 1, 2028 [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large freight railroads — through the annual $1 million fee, the new detectors, stricter inspection requirements, and tenfold-higher fines — and tank car owners facing an earlier phase-out. Those costs would partly pass through to shippers and, eventually, freight prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large freight railroads and tank car owners

drawbacks.text: The bill's costs fall on the railroads, which would likely pass some of them to shippers and eventually to consumer prices; the 10-mile hotbox detector mandate alone is a large capital requirement for carriers [S3].

The bill requires rulemaking tied to the National Transportation Safety Board's East Palestine report and to a one-year deadline, so actual protections would depend on how quickly the Department of Transportation writes and enforces the rules [S3].

Only Class I railroads pay the $1 million training fee and only Class I railroads face the 10-mile detector spacing requirement, so smaller railroads operating hazmat trains are treated more lightly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case was concrete: the bill responded to the East Palestine derailment, and its detector-spacing, inspection, and notice provisions target the exact failures that crash exposed — including covering trains that fall outside existing high-hazard train rules. The costs are real but concentrated on an industry that could absorb them; the main honest caveat is that higher fines and mandates only protect people if the Department writes and enforces the rules promptly, and the bill gives it deadlines but no extra enforcement staff.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Railroads subcommittee in March 2023, and it sat there — no markup, no vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Johnson of Ohio introduced the bill on March 17, 2023, joined by ten members of the Ohio delegation from both parties, after the February 2023 East Palestine derailment in his district [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on March 17, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials on March 20, 2023 [S5].
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, 8 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but no further action was recorded in the House [S4] [S5].
On January 29, 2024, Rep. Emilia Sykes of Ohio took over first sponsorship so cosponsors could keep being added after Rep. Johnson, but the bill still never received a committee or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest freight railroads came out ahead: they avoided the $1 million annual fee, the tenfold-higher fines, the mandatory hotbox detectors every 10 miles, the stricter inspection requirements, and the earlier tank-car phase-out that the bill would have imposed on them.

for.name: Bill Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the RAIL Act and rounded up ten Ohio colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Assumed first sponsorship in January 2024 to keep adding cosponsors after Johnson.

against.name: Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee: after referral on March 17, 2023 and subcommittee referral on March 20, 2023, no markup, hearing vote, or floor action was ever recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backing was bipartisan from the start — ten original cosponsors from Ohio's delegation of both parties — and its later cosponsor list split 8 Democrats to 7 Republicans; no recorded vote ever showed opposition because none was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would have charged each big railroad a $1 million annual fee, raised maximum safety fines tenfold, required hotbox detectors every 10 miles, and tightened inspection requirements. Its death spared them those costs; the public benefit of those requirements is what the industry avoided paying for.
The bill moved the phase-out of older DOT-111 tank cars for flammable liquids up one year, to May 1, 2028, forcing earlier retirement or retrofit of equipment the industry would otherwise use longer.

industries.industry: Hotbox detector manufacturers and rail-safety contractors
industries.note: A mandate for a detector on every 10-mile hazmat segment would have created a large new market for wayside detection equipment, in step with the public's interest in catching wheel-bearing failures before derailments.
